Indonesia is home to over 1.800 bird species, including the Helmeted Hornbill (Rangkong Gading – Rhinoplax
vigil) and the Cendrawasih (Bird of Paradise – Paradisaea apoda).
The Helmeted Hornbill is a very large forest bird native to Sumatra and Kalimantan. It has blackish-brown
feathers, a white belly, and two remarkably long central tail feathers that can reach up to 120 cm in length. Its
most distinctive feature is its solid red casque (helm gading) on top of its beak, which accounts for 11% of its
body weight! Male hornbills use this solid casque in mid-air head-to-head clashes to defend fruit trees. During
the nesting season, the female hornbill seals herself inside a high tree cavity using mud and fruit pulp, leaving
only a narrow slit through which the male feeds her and their chick for months. Tragically, the Helmeted Hornbill
is listed as Critically Endangered because it is poached for its solid casque.
Meanwhile, the Greater Bird of Paradise (Cendrawasih) is native to Papua and the Aru Islands. Male Cen-
drawasih birds are famous for their dazzling golden-yellow crown, emerald-green throat, and fluffy yellow-and-
white flank plumes used in elaborate courtship dances.

In Unit 2 of English for Nusantara Grade 9, Galang and Andre interviewed Mr. Rahmat about how school life in
the 1990s differed from digital life in 2026:
• Searching for Information: In the 1990s, students used to go to the town library and flip through thick
printed encyclopedias and card catalogs to write a school paper. They did not have search engines or AI.
• Communication: Teenagers used to send handwritten letters via post office or queue at coin-operated
public payphones (telepon umum koin). If they wanted to send a short urgent message, people used a pager
(beeper).
• Entertainment & Music: Friends used to record their favorite songs from the radio onto magnetic cassette
tapes and rewind the tape using a wooden pencil when the ribbon got loose!
• Photos: Families used to use analog film cameras (36 exposures per roll) and had to wait days at a photo
studio to print the pictures before they could see the results.

How to Make an Eco-Friendly Denim Desk Organizer:
Materials: 1 clean tin can, a piece of old blue jeans (denim fabric), multipurpose glue, scissors, and batik
ribbon.
Steps: (1) Wash and dry the used tin can thoroughly, ensuring there are no sharp edges on the rim. (2)
Measure and cut the old denim fabric to fit around the tin can. (3) Apply glue evenly onto the outside of the
can and wrap the denim fabric tightly around it. (4) Glue a strip of traditional batik ribbon around the top and
